papers.title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
papers.abstract: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.

papers.title: CENTRY: A Probabilistic Latent-State Model for Continual AI Risk Estimation, Monitoring, and Regulation
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. A structured latent-variable model is developed in which the latent representation is decomposed into a fast interaction subspace that captures the evolving AI--environment dynamics and three slow latent subspaces that encode the long-term risk states associated with the dataset, hardware, and model components. Rather than requiring a ground-truth risk label at every time step, the component-risk states are treated as latent variables and are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally informed during training and continual refinement by evidence-supported behavior--cause records. The resulting framework unifies continual probabilistic inference, online risk estimation, and adaptive risk regulation in an implementable architecture. Under the explicit assumptions stated for the corresponding results, we establish formal guarantees spanning safety, learning, inference, and operations, including finite-horizon and asymptotic risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, consistency and identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay, false-alarm, containment, and computational-complexity characterizations.

papers.title: Unlocking Heterogeneous Accelerator Flexibility in AI Data Centers: Sizing and Workload Allocation
papers.abstract: AI data centers are an emerging electricity demand, but limited local grid capacity could delay their connection and expansion. While existing operational strategies consider spatio-temporal workload flexibility, few studies address the strategic sizing and allocation of diverse accelerator archetypes with different capital and energy-efficiency trade-offs. This paper unlocks the flexibility potential of heterogeneous accelerators by jointly sizing and allocating different AI workloads (training, delay-tolerant batch work, and online inference requests) across sites and hours to meet the time-varying grid constraint at minimum cost. Workload-specific throughput and energy coefficients link these decisions to facility power. In a representative two-site case, heterogeneous sizing reduces daily cost by 6.5% relative to spatio-temporal scheduling with fixed capacity. When evaluated using workload-specific performance, a capacity design based on workload-averaged hardware coefficients costs 7.7% more than the proposed design. The proposed design also eliminates the envelope violations of an unconstrained design at a 0.25\% daily cost increase. These results show how hardware heterogeneity and workload flexibility jointly shape economical, grid-compliant capacity plans.

papers.title: What Graph Unlearning Cannot Erase: Physics-Induced Leakage of Cyberattack Information in Electric Vehicle Charging Networks
papers.abstract: Electric vehicle charging stations (EVCSs) can expose distribution feeders to cyberattacks. While machine learning methods, including graph neural networks (GNNs), can localize which bus is compromised, significant challenges remain in data sharing and model training. For example, data-sharing agreements grant EVCS operators the right to withdraw their charging power for privacy or security reasons from a deployed model, yet retraining from scratch on every request would repeat the full-retraining (FR) cost. To address this, we study graph unlearning (GU) for EVCS cyberattack localization, formulated as a feature-level unlearning problem on a graph-level multi-label classification task. We benchmark fine-tuning (FT) against two GU baselines on the IEEE 34-bus, 123-bus, and 8500-node distribution networks across three GNN backbones and cumulative unlearning scenarios. Experiments show that a GNN unlearned or retrained without the withdrawn power still localizes cyberattacks at the forgotten EVCSs. This physics-induced leakage floor arises because a cyberattack on an EVCS also shifts the voltages of electrically coupled buses. The distribution system operator can thus promise an EVCS operator that the deployed GNN model no longer uses its charging power data, but the voltages still reveal cyberattacks at its EVCS.

papers.title: DNN-Assisted Deterministic Policy Learning for Adaptive IRS-NOMA-OWC Networks
papers.abstract: Intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) has been considered a promising technology in optical wireless communication (OWC) networks due to its potential to overcome the line-of-sight (LoS) blockage issue and enhance coverage. In this paper, a dynamic IRS-assisted indoor non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA)-OWC network is modeled, and an optimization problem is formulated to maximize the sum rate subject to the quality-of-service (QoS) requirements of multiple mobile users, by jointly optimizing the power allocation and the IRS mirror orientations, from which the user's decoding order is induced rather than being fixed. Since the problem is non-convex and the channel conditions vary with user mobility, conventional optimization methods may incur considerable computational overhead. Therefore, a two-stage deep neural network-deep reinforcement learning (DNN-DRL) framework is proposed. In the first stage, the DNN estimates the user's positions and orientations in real time, removing the need for perfect knowledge of the user state. In the second stage, a deterministic policy gradient (DPG)-based DRL algorithm uses these estimates to jointly optimize the power allocation and IRS mirror orientations, with the decoding order updated according to the resulting effective channel gains. The results show that the proposed framework approaches the performance upper bounds and outperforms standard DRL algorithms, conventional optimization methods, and deployments without IRS in terms of sum rate and fairness, while achieving faster convergence. Furthermore, online adaptation of the decoding order maintains higher QoS satisfaction than a fixed decoding order, particularly under high user mobility.

papers.title: Seabird-Aware Multi-Objective Offshore Wind Capacity Allocation: A Gippsland Case Study
papers.abstract: Offshore wind planning requires balancing capital cost, wind-resource potential, and seabird exposure. We formulate a spatial tri-objective mixed-integer linear program for offshore wind capacity allocation, minimizing capital cost and modeled seabird exposure while maximizing wind-weighted capacity. Applied to Australia's Gippsland offshore wind area, the model identifies exposure reductions of 23-44% at capital-cost premiums of 0.8-6.1% across 15 wind-weighted capacity requirements. We benchmark exposure-aware optimization against 19 percentile-based exclusion thresholds. At a fixed wind-weighted capacity requirement, the 5th-percentile threshold reduces exposure by 30.1% at a 37.6% cost premium, versus at least 30.1% at a 1.4% premium with optimization. Under a fixed capital budget, exclusion screening reduces exposure by 48.2% with a 26.9% capacity loss, compared with 48.5% and 7.6%, respectively, under optimization. These results highlight the value of explicitly optimizing graded seabird exposure.

papers.title: Learned Network Dynamics for Model Predictive Traffic Signal Control under Incidents
papers.abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) of urban traffic signals relies on a model of how queues respond to signal decisions, which is hard to specify and calibrate in heterogeneous networks, particularly when incidents change capacities and turning shares. Measurements add a second limitation: the controlled lanes at the stop line are often short, so queues extending upstream of them fall outside lane-level measurements. We propose GNN-MPC, a receding-horizon controller that plans with action-conditioned network dynamics learned by graph neural networks. Phase sequences are coordinated across intersections by approximate best responses, with an acceptance test that keeps the predicted cost no higher than that of the initial plan. In microscopic simulation under non-recurrent incidents, GNN-MPC reduces travel time and increases completed trips relative to all tested controllers, on a homogeneous grid and a heterogeneous 21-intersection network. Controlled comparisons on the heterogeneous network distinguish the roles of observation and prediction. With nearly as many vehicles entering the network, GNN-MPC reduces travel time by 13% relative to MaxPressure with the same upstream measurement, and GNN-MPC without the upstream representation does not reproduce its performance. Under the same traffic measurements, planner and objective, replacing the learned dynamics with calibrated store-and-forward predictors increases travel time by 31-34%. Observing hidden demand and predicting its response to control are thus complementary requirements of network-level predictive control.

papers.title: Loop-OPF: Solver-Informed Learning for Optimal Power Flow with Inference-Time Topology Adaptivity
papers.abstract: Learning for optimal power flow (OPF) has recently been advocated to accelerate OPF solutions by using a pre-trained neural network (NN) to predict directly from given inputs such as the load demand. However, existing learning-for-OPF methods largely fall short of ensuring the optimality and feasibility of their predictions. They also struggle to adapt at inference time to unseen topology scenarios, such as those caused by line or generator outages. This work puts forth Loop-OPF, a solver-informed NN that builds its layers from the iterations of the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method. Under standard convexity and regularity conditions on DC-OPF, the resultant fixed-point output of Loop-OPF is thus optimal and feasible. To speed up PDHG across diverse OPF scenarios, Loop-OPF learns certain PDHG parameters in a self-supervised manner, without any OPF solution labels. We adopt the deep equilibrium (DEQ) framework for training so that the memory cost does not grow with the number of layers. As the grid topology enters every layer as an input, the same trained Loop-OPF directly adapts to unseen contingencies without retraining. Numerical tests on the IEEE 300-bus and PEGASE 1354-, 2869-, and 9241-bus networks have demonstrated the accuracy and topology adaptivity of the proposed Loop-OPF over competing learning-for-OPF methods.

papers.title: Error-Corrected Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Optimal Control of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles under Uncertainty
papers.abstract: We solve open-loop optimal control problems under parametric uncertainty using a physics-informed DeepONet that returns trajectories for all sampled scenarios in one evaluation. Trained only on the residual at generic controls, the operator is reused across targets and horizons. Because a gradient-based optimizer exploits surrogate errors, we correct the prediction by one Newton step on the dynamics, computed for all scenarios and times by one parallel scan. The corrected state has a second-order error bounded by the residual alone, and the corrected cost is honest for every control up to the sampling error. On a fixed-wing UAV benchmark, the corrected operator matches the accuracy of a batched Adam solver and an Ipopt solver at equal sample size and is 8 times faster than the Adam solver on the same GPU at a few hundred scenarios and 15 times faster than Ipopt on a CPU.

papers.title: Where Delay Compensation Belongs in a Decentralized Mean-Field-Game Swarm with a Control-Barrier Safety Filter
papers.abstract: Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Neighbors are known only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every estimate, grows with swarm size. In simulation this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Without delay, swarms of up to 100 agents do not collide, even with each measurement's noise held for a whole frame; with it, stale estimates at the CBF cause collisions beyond a frame period of 125 to 175 ms, or 75 to 100 ms at 100 agents with held noise, and swarm size sets where that limit lies and how steeply collisions rise. At the MFG, staleness makes the local density noisier without biasing it, and throughput drops by at most a tenth. We then compensate with lightweight on-board predictors, from constant-velocity fits to a small learned network, that estimate each neighbor's position from its last broadcasts. A layer-split experiment shows where prediction is needed: at the CBF it restores safety and extends the tolerated frame period by 1.4 to 1.7 times with an untrained constant-velocity fit and about 2.3 with the learned network when the noise is redrawn each step; with noise held for a frame the two extend it about equally, while at the MFG it only refines the congestion correction. A constant wider safety margin, the simplest alternative, makes collisions more frequent in a bottleneck. With the routing solved offline, that layer is robust to the delay because it sees neighbors only through a crowd average; compensation belongs in the safety filter, switched on only above the uncompensated limit, since below it the predictor's own error adds collisions.

papers.title: Energy-preserving Bayesian model reduction: closed-form structured posteriors and probabilistic stability certificates for quadratic operator inference
papers.abstract: Bayesian operator inference learns reduced-order models (ROMs) with polynomial structure from state data and returns a closed-form Gaussian posterior over the reduced operators. That posterior is unconstrained, so it gives positive probability to operators with unbounded dynamics, and current practice controls this only through finite-horizon simulation tests on a few samples. We show that energy preservation of the quadratic operator is a set of linear equality constraints, which can be imposed exactly inside the Bayesian formulation without losing the closed form. In particular, the constrained posterior follows from one Kalman-type update of the unconstrained one, and its samples are obtained exactly, by the same correction applied to unconstrained draws. Under this structure, global boundedness for all initial conditions and bounded inputs reduces to a linear matrix condition on the symmetric part of the linear operator. The simulation test is then replaced by a probabilistic stability certificate: the posterior probability that the ROM is globally bounded, estimated with exact confidence bounds; the posterior restricted to certified models is then sampled exactly by rejection. For energy-conserving systems, the linear part can be constrained to be skew-symmetric as well: every draw then grows at most linearly in time, and conserves energy exactly when unforced. On a forced viscous Burgers' equation, the Korteweg-de Vries equation and a two-dimensional viscous Burgers' equation, every sample of the constrained posterior integrates to a bounded trajectory, where up to all unconstrained draws diverge, and beyond the observation window the former is also the more accurate of the two.

papers.title: Binary Decision Process in Pre-Evacuation Behavior
papers.abstract: In crowd evacuation the time interval before decisive movement towards a safe place is defined as the pre-evacuation phase, and it has crucial impact on the total time required for safe egress. This process mainly refers to situation awareness and response to an external stressors, e.g., fire alarms. Due to the complexity of human cognitive process, simulation is used to study this important time interval. In this paper a binary decision process is formulated to simulate pre-evacuation time of many evacuees in a given social context. The model combines the classic opinion dynamics (the French-DeGroot model) with binary phase transition to describe how group pre-evacuation time emerges from individual interaction. The model parameters are quantitatively meaningful to human factors research within socio-psychological background, e.g., whether an individual is stubborn or open-minded, or what kind of the social topology exists among the individuals and how it matters in aggregating individuals into social groups. The modeling framework also describes collective motion of many evacuee agents in a planar space, and the resulting multi-agent system is partly similar to the Vicsek flocking model, and it is meaningful to explore complex social behavior during phase transition of a non-equilibrium process.

papers.title: FORTH: Grounding Tactile VLA Execution via Forward-Only Proxy-Control Pairing
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are widely credited with force control, operating on the unverified assumption that proxy loss minimization implies physical force grounding. In this work, we demonstrate that this assumption breaks down at three core deployment levels: frozen visual backbones discard contact geometry, downstream losses mask token-level gradient alignment, and discrete indicators trigger optimization collapse. To address these disconnections, we present FORTH, a forward-only measurement harness and execution framework that explicitly pairs the optimization objective at each level with its physical control observable. FORTH incorporates three grounded pillars: a layer-local, forward-only tactile encoder that preserves spatial contact geometry without backpropagation, a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter enabling activation-space updates, and SlipGuard, a continuous tactile verification gate that fires on incipient slip. On an elasto-plastic structural shell, FORTH's closed-loop gate peaks at 29 times lower grip force than a monotone reflex ramp, preventing structural crush where the baseline leaves permanent deformation. Furthermore, FORTH matches state-of-the-art execution performance with a 97.6% average success rate across three evaluated LIBERO suites, while reducing peak activation memory by 7.12 times compared to a backpropagated step on the same backbone. Enhanced perception enables deeper physical intelligence.

papers.title: Search-Informed MPPI for Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Monte Carlo Tree Expansion
papers.abstract: Kinodynamic motion planning in large-scale, cluttered environments remains challenging, as dynamically feasible, collision-free trajectories must be computed efficiently over long horizons. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) can strategically explore long-horizon alternatives but faces large branching factors in continuous control spaces and often relies on random default-policy rollouts, whereas Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) efficiently optimizes local trajectories yet remains susceptible to obstacle-induced local minima. To overcome these challenges, we propose Search-Informed MPPI (SI-MPPI), a unified framework that embeds MPPI trajectory optimization within MCTS-based tree search. The core concept is to fuse the expansion and default-policy simulation stages of MCTS into a single MPPI expansion stage guided by structured intermediate targets, termed baits. During each expansion, an adaptive bait-handling rule retains geometrically valid baits as local targets for GPU-batched MPPI optimizations that generate dynamically feasible candidate motion segments. Feasibility gating then checks these candidates for collision safety and sufficient progress, and top-$k$ selection admits the lowest-cost accepted candidates as tree edges, yielding sparse, directed tree growth; thereafter, effective sample size (ESS)-guided adaptation warm-starts subsequent expansions, while cost-based backpropagation updates tree statistics. Extensive simulations across four large-scale, cluttered 2D occupancy-grid maps demonstrate that SI-MPPI consistently produces the smallest search trees and smoothest angular control profiles compared with three kinodynamic baselines, while maintaining competitive planning times and path lengths. Ablation results further highlight the importance of GPU batching, adaptive bait handling, and retaining multiple expansion candidates for planning efficiency and robustness.

papers.title: Connectivity-Constrained Linear System Realization: Feasibility and Realizable Sets
papers.abstract: In this paper, we first study the problem of finding a state-space realization of a given transfer function that adheres to a given connectivity pattern (i.e., support). While variants of this problem have been studied in distributed and structured control, existing work typically focuses on connectivity patterns relating to some networked plant. In contrast, we are interested in arbitrary connectivity patterns, which are relevant to modeling problems in sensorimotor neuroscience. We show that this problem is equivalent to solving a system of multivariate polynomial equations, and can be solved exactly without relaxation or approximation. We then study the reverse problem: given a connectivity pattern, what transfer functions have a state-space realization that adheres to this pattern? In other words, what transfer functions can this pattern realize? A surprising finding is that any given pattern can realize nearly all transfer functions, or very few transfer functions. We provide rigorous results and algorithms for both problems, leveraging technical machinery from algebraic geometry. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated in examples at the end of the paper.

papers.title: $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ Grid-Forming Control in DC Microgrids
papers.abstract: The growing share of DC-based generation, storage and loads has increased interest in DC microgrids. As a result, DC-bus voltage regulation and stability have become active research topics, with considerable effort directed at improving the transient performance of conventional droop control. Although numerous variants of droop algorithms have been proposed, many rely on increasingly complex control structures with multiple tuning parameters and measurements, thereby increasing the commissioning burden. Moreover, stable interaction with the surrounding microgrid is not guaranteed by design. To address these issues, this paper develops a passivity-constrained $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ synthesis method for the DC-bus voltage controller. The proposed $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ controller emulates the desired grid-forming behavior of the converter by minimizing the $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ error norm between device-level performance indices and their desired values, while additionally enforcing passivity during the optimization. The novel $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ control scheme is benchmarked in the frequency domain against representative droop-based and virtual-DC-machine algorithms from the literature, while experiments on a four-converter DC microgrid corroborate the frequency-domain analysis and validate the practical applicability of the algorithm.

papers.title: Mode Recommendation and Dynamic Routing Guidance for Improved Trip Quality in Mixed Traffic Networks
papers.abstract: Urban mixed traffic networks provide diverse mobility options, yet conventional routing guidance with fixed travel modes leaves the benefits of coordinating travel modes and route planning largely unexploited. This paper proposes an integrated mode recommendation and dynamic routing guidance framework for urban mixed traffic networks comprising private vehicles, autonomous vehicles, and buses. We formulate a dynamic trip index (DTX) that incorporates mode-specific travel time, monetary cost, and convenience, enabling consistent evaluation of trip quality across travel modes. Using this measure, we develop a mode recommendation method that selects feasible autonomous vehicle or bus services based on predicted DTX for travelers without private vehicles, while preserving service capacity for travelers with known demand. We integrate this method with dynamic routing guidance for private and autonomous vehicles to improve the average trip quality of all travelers. Simulation studies involving $1{,}500$ travelers on a real-world road network in Shanghai, China, show that the proposed framework increases the mean realized DTX by $13.01\%$ compared with dynamic routing guidance alone and by $19.68\%$ compared with fixed travel modes with preplanned routes, highlighting the value of mode flexibility in improving trip quality beyond route adaptation.

papers.title: Which Data-Center Load Models Can Be Trusted? An Evidence-Graded Review of Dynamic Modeling and Validation for Large Computational Loads
papers.abstract: Grid operators now require dynamic models of data centers and other large computational loads, and new ride-through rules assume that these models predict how facilities respond to disturbances. This review asks what evidence supports that assumption. We coded 160 documents, screened from 1,424 de-duplicated database and seed records plus 65 added documents, by the strongest reference object each presents, from grid-side records to simulation only. Across 19 field-evidence entries, 15 requirement documents from three continents and nine model classes, we find two comparisons of a standard library model with measured data-center events: with default parameters the model failed both, and refitting it to each event separately reduced the error but was never tested on an unseen event. Among the sources reviewed, we found no successful held-out validation of a frozen, facility-specific data-center model against an independent measured disturbance, and 25 of the 33 model-phenomenon combinations with any evidence involve no electrical measurement. The features that distinguish the new rules (memory of repeated dips, recovery within 0.5-3 s, proportional power reduction during the sag, overvoltage response) are those current phasor models cannot represent or have never been tested against. In the operator procedures examined, simulations and model-to-model benchmarks are accepted as evidence of model fidelity, unlike the measured validation required of generators, and proposed mitigations have mostly been evaluated on unvalidated facility models. We propose context-of-use gates that separate calibration from validation, release labels for model claims, a minimum validation protocol with acceptance criteria, and a research agenda.

papers.title: Strong Functional Observability and Strong Functional Detectability: Applications to Functional Observer Design for Systems with Unknown Inputs
papers.abstract: This paper investigates strong functional observability, strong functional detectability, and strong$^*$ functional detectability for continuous-time linear systems with unknown inputs in both the state and measurement equations. Extending Kratz's finite algebraic approach \cite{26}, zero-output trajectories are characterized through the projected kernel of a finite matrix, without differentiating the unknown inputs. This characterization yields a necessary and sufficient rank condition for strong functional observability. For strong functional detectability, a frequency-dependent rank criterion involving only the original system matrices is derived, along with an equivalent finite test based on reduced zero-output dynamics. Strong$^*$ functional detectability is then characterized by an additional algebraic rank condition, and its relationship with the existence of stable functional observers is examined. A constructive observer design procedure based on constrained Sylvester equations is also developed. Particular cases and a numerical process example illustrate the theoretical results.

papers.title: Network Traffic Dynamics in Urban Low-Altitude Air Transport with Projected-Space Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams
papers.abstract: The growth of Low-Altitude Air Transport (LAAT) systems calls for effective macroscopic modeling tools to manage dense drone traffic. The Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD) offers a promising framework for this purpose, but its conventional formulations do not directly account for the three-dimensional interactions and path deviations that characterize drone operations. To address this challenge, we introduce a projected-space framework that represents drone motion using projected speed and shortest origin-destination (OD) distances, eliminating the dependence on realized trip lengths that are unknown at trip generation. Under suitable assumptions, we prove the steady-state exactness of the projected-space accumulation-based model and establish deterministic finite-window error bounds for the trip-based estimator. The projected-space accumulation-based formulation is further extended to heterogeneous multi-class systems to accommodate different drone characteristics and operational priorities. Microscopic simulations validate the projected-space formulations under stationary and transient traffic conditions, including hysteresis. Moreover, simulations involving heterogeneous priority classes demonstrate that mixed-priority operations can improve network outflow under the investigated scenarios. These findings establish a theoretical foundation for projected-space macroscopic modeling of LAAT systems and support its application to real-time traffic estimation and future airspace management and control.

papers.title: Active Learning of Flows from Curve Observations using Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: The active learning of real control systems requires informative roll-outs of controls. In this paper, we present a local optimization algorithm that finds the trajectory that most reduces uncertainty about the flow of a control system modeled by a Gaussian process. Therefore, we derive an approximation scheme for the posterior kernel of the Gaussian process after observing it on an entire continuous-time trajectory and establish a Pontryagin-type necessary condition for the optimizer. As the flow is unknown, the actual trajectory can deviate from the planned trajectory. We propose a trajectory planner that searches for the most informative control within a maximal allowed deviation horizon instead of a fixed time horizon. We show by trajectory-wise time rescaling that the underlying optimal control problem is equivalent to a fixed end time optimal control problem. Finally, we study both the fixed end time planner and the fixed maximum deviation planner in a numerical example and compare them with benchmarks.

papers.title: Linear Quadratic Control With Event-Based Control Actions: Performance Beyond Periodic Control
papers.abstract: This paper investigates linear quadratic (LQ) control for discrete-time stochastic systems to balance control performance and actuation rate. In our framework, the control input is sparse in time, and the actuation timings are determined in an event-based manner. We examine two types of problems: A sparsity-promoting regularization problem and a hard-constraint problem with a prescribed average actuation rate. Due to the combinatorial nature of these problems, finding optimal solutions is generally hard. Inspired by rollout algorithms in the context of dynamic programming, we develop a rollout-based approach to obtain tractable suboptimal policies. We show closed-loop stability and establish theoretical performance guarantees with respect to classical periodic control. Moreover, under additional conditions, we quantify the performance improvement over periodic control and prove that this improvement is strictly positive. A numerical example demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method in balancing control performance and actuation rate.

papers.title: Incentive-based Fleet Rebalancing in Vehicle-Sharing Systems via Equilibrium-Constrained Optimal Control
papers.abstract: We propose an incentive-based fleet rebalancing scheme for vehicle-sharing systems that uses fare discounts to steer users toward alternative pick-up locations. The discounts solve an optimal control problem that trades off users leaving the service against incentive costs over a day of operation. Users' responses to incentives are modeled as a Nash equilibrium of logit models coupled through shared vehicle-availability constraints, which makes the control problem a mathematical program with nested equilibrium constraints. We develop a first-order algorithm that backpropagates through the equilibria via nonsmooth implicit differentiation and enjoys convergence guarantees. In a case study that uses Helsinki bike-sharing data, our scheme reduces the number of leaving users by up to 99% relative to no incentives, and outperforms heuristic policies while using up to 52% less incentive.

papers.title: Planar Formation Control with Minimal Sensing and No Common Orientation: An Almost-Global Result
papers.abstract: Formation control based on geometric constraints often requires either rigid interaction graphs or a common orientation reference. This paper investigates whether a prescribed planar formation can instead be achieved using only $N-1$ pairwise interactions while preserving global rotational freedom. To this end, a guiding-vector-field-inspired framework is developed in which each selected distance relation is represented by a parameterized circular manifold and the remaining geometric freedom is coordinated through relative virtual phases, based on which, a distributed controller is then constructed. The closed-loop system is shown to possess only the desired equilibrium set and a degenerate undesired equilibrium set corresponding to collapse of the central edge. The latter is proved to form a saddle-type equilibrium manifold with a measure-zero stable set, yielding almost-global convergence to the desired formation. In addition, the controller admits an implementation under mutually misaligned local frames using locally expressed relative measurements and scalar phase information.

papers.title: Hierarchical Agentic Mid-Band Agility for Reliable Low-Latency Space-Air-Ground Integrated V2X Networks
papers.abstract: Upper-mid-band spectrum offers bandwidth opportunities for the integrated networks of ground vehicles, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites to support 6G wide-area vehicle-to-everything (V2X) connectivity. However, V2X services' latency and reliability are sensitive to the mid-band selection due to frequency-dependent propagation and rain attenuation. This paper investigates environment-aware spectrum agility over candidate frequency range 3 (FR3) bands within 7.125-24.25 GHz, jointly with end-to-end (E2E) multi-path traffic splitting and transmit power control. Each data packet is partitioned into non-overlapping subflows over direct and UAV-assisted paths, with failed sky-link subflows selectively retransmitted subject to retransmission and freshness constraints. We formulate latency- and reliability-oriented problems, followed by a unified sequential optimization problem incorporating band-switching costs and average quality-of-service (QoS) violation budgets. To coordinate optimization decisions across heterogeneous timescales, we develop an agentic AI-assisted hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning (AA-HMARL) framework. A high-level agentic supervisor integrates recurrent memory, analytical evaluation of candidate bands, and event-triggered replanning to coordinate slow environmental adaptation with fast channel and retransmission dynamics, while distributed ground vehicles and UAV agents optimize data splitting and power using constrained MAPPO. Simulation results demonstrate an adjustable reliability-latency trade-off. Particularly, AA-HMARL reduces the mean E2E completion latency and the mean number of retransmission rounds among successfully delivered updates by 17.8-25.5% and 57.6-61.5%, respectively, and reduces the mean age of information (AoI) by 12.7-14.6% relative to fixed-band MAPPO across two traffic types.

papers.title: On Robust Strictly Positive Real Synthesis for High-Order Interval Polynomials
papers.abstract: We establish two complementary results on common strictly positive real (SPR) numerators for Hurwitz-stable interval polynomial families. First, for every order $n \ge 10$, we construct a monic Hurwitz-stable interval polynomial family with rational endpoints and positive width in every nonleading coefficient such that every nonzero real numerator of degree at most $n$ produces a strictly negative real part at some member and some positive frequency. In particular, robust Hurwitz stability alone does not guarantee equal-degree SPR synthesis in high orders. Second, for every order $n \ge 1$, we prove that a common real SPR numerator of exact degree $n$ always exists whenever the lower endpoint of each interior coefficient interval is at most $10^{-5}$ times its upper endpoint, while the constant and leading coefficients vary over arbitrary compact positive intervals.

papers.title: Iteration-Dependent Temporal Resilience in Diffusion Models for Approximate Computing
papers.abstract: This paper empirically analyzes iteration-dependent resilience in diffusion models by replacing MACs with efficient SAC approximations. Results on Q-Diffusion show early steps are highly sensitive while later steps are robust, enabling iteration- aware approximation that improves efficiency and reduces hardware cost with minimal quality loss.

papers.title: Eliminating Make-Whole Uplifts with a Minimum-Cost Uniform Price Adder
papers.abstract: Co-optimizing energy and flexible ramping reserves may dispatch generators at locational marginal prices (LMPs) below their submitted energy offer prices, necessitating out-of-market make-whole payments. Such payments create discriminatory settlements among generators and may incentivize strategic bidding for higher profits. This paper proposes LMP+U, an in-market uniform price adder to LMP for transmission-constrained networks, which minimizes demand payments subject to zero out-of-market make-whole uplift, preserves LMP-based congestion charges, and provides locally truthful bidding incentives for price-taking generators. We also identify conditions under which a price-taking generator can increase its profit by inflating its energy offer under conventional LMP with make-whole uplift. Numerical simulations illustrate the properties of LMP+U and its advantages over conventional LMP in congested networks.

papers.title: Bayesian Bias Learning-Enabled Probabilistic Voltage Estimation with Unknown Uncertainty Modeling of DERs in Distribution Grids
papers.abstract: One key challenge in distribution system state es- timation is unknown input statistics from the growing inte- gration of distributed energy resources (DERs), which may largely deviate from Gaussian uncertainty. Existing model-based estimators often rely on the assumption that all inputs follow known Gaussian distributions, while data-driven methods suffer from overfitting and failure in out-of-distribution scenarios. This paper proposes a Bayesian bias learning (BBL)-enabled probabilistic voltage estimation method in distribution systems with unknown DER generation statistics. The proposed learning- enabled method consists of two stages: probabilistic uncertainty inference and computationally efficient voltage estimation. First, a physics-constrained probabilistic density inference network is developed to learn Gaussian mixture representations of DER generation from historical data. Then, the resulting probabilistic representations, treated as pseudo-measurements, are integrated into a BBL-enabled voltage estimator via a decomposition- and-parallelization mechanism. Furthermore, utilizing a linear analytical solution, the proposed BBL-enabled voltage estimator efficiently captures linearization-induced biases and attains ac- curate probabilistic estimation. By integrating learning-enabled probabilistic uncertainty modeling into the parallel estimation structure, the proposed method achieves uncertainty-aware scal- able voltage estimation. Case studies on two unbalanced IEEE distribution networks show that the proposed estimator achieves significantly higher accuracy and computational efficiency under unknown uncertainty, outperforming recent data-driven and model-based methods.

papers.title: Load-Following Dynamics of an SMR-Powered All-Electric Ship with Battery Energy Storage
papers.abstract: Small modular reactors (SMRs) are being considered as compact, high-energy-density power sources for future all-electric ships. In such systems, propulsion-load variations can propagate through the electrical network, turbine-generator set, steam generator, and reactor, producing coupled nuclear, thermal, mechanical, and electrical transients. This paper presents an integrated dynamic load-following analysis of an SMR-powered all-electric ship with and without battery energy storage system (BESS) support. The model couples an integral pressurized water reactor, a once-through moving-boundary steam generator, a simplified turbine model, a synchronous generator, an AC shipboard electrical network, an asynchronous propulsion motor, and a grid-connected BESS. A propulsion-load reduction is applied through the motor torque command, and the responses of the SMR-alone and SMR+BESS configurations are compared. The results show that, without BESS support, the sudden decrease in propulsion motor power creates a temporary surplus between turbine mechanical power and electrical demand, causing a large over-frequency transient and rapid steam-cycle adjustment. With BESS support, the battery absorbs excess electrical power during the transient, reducing the frequency peak from approximately 61.1 Hz to about 60.06 Hz. The BESS also indirectly smooths the upstream steam-cycle and reactor responses, including steam flow, steam-generator pressure, feedwater flow, coolant temperature, reactivity, reactor thermal power, and steam-generator region lengths. These results demonstrate the importance of modeling nuclear-powered electric ships as coupled multi-domain systems and show that BESS integration can improve short-term load-following performance.
